name: OPA1692IDR
title: OPA1692: dual low-power, low-noise, low-distortion audio op amp
summary: The OPA1692 holds two unity-gain-stable audio op amps, each drawing 650 µA typical, with 4.2 nV/√Hz input noise at 1 kHz and –127 dB THD+N at 1 kHz (3 VRMS, 2 kΩ). It runs from 3.5 V to 36 V single or ±1.75 V to ±18 V split supplies, the output swings to within about 200 mV of each rail into 2 kΩ, and it can source and sink about 50 mA. Gain-bandwidth is 5.1 MHz and slew rate 23 V/µs. It comes in an 8-pin SOIC (D) and an 8-pin VSSOP (DGK); OPA1692IDR is the SOIC on a 2500-piece reel.

circuits.title: Low-noise preamplifier for 3-wire electret microphones
circuits.description: One channel of the OPA1692 on ±5 V amplifies a Primo EM-173 three-wire electret capsule, aimed at a battery wireless microphone: 120 dB SPL maximum, 20 Hz to 20 kHz, better than 75 dB SNR, under 1.5 mA in all. The capsule takes 5 V and its signal line is loaded by R1 in parallel with R2 (5.6 kΩ above 20 Hz, as the capsule wants). C1 couples the signal in and sets a 20 Hz high-pass with R2. R3 and C2 form a 15.9 MHz low-pass that keeps RF out of the input. The amplifier is noninverting: R4 equals R2 so the bias current sees the same DC resistance at both inputs, and C3 makes the DC gain 1. In the audio band the gain is 1 + R5/R6 = 12 (21.6 dB), so a 20 Pa peak from the capsule reaches the ±4.8 V linear swing; C4 across R5 rolls the gain off at 20 kHz. Measured: 11.79 V/V, 24 Hz to 21 kHz, 79.3 dB SNR (1 Pa, A-weighted), 1.25 mA (600 µA capsule plus 650 µA amplifier).

circuits.title: Two-wire electret microphone preamplifier
circuits.description: The 3-wire preamplifier reworked for a two-wire electret capsule, whose internal JFET has no source resistor. A 2.2 kΩ resistor from 5 V biases the capsule and the audio appears across it. A 0.1 µF capacitor and a 47 kΩ resistor to ground couple it into one OPA1692 channel through a 100 Ω / 100 pF RF filter. The channel is noninverting on ±5 V: 47 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, 2.2 µF from there to the gain node, 150 Ω from the gain node to ground, and 3.57 kΩ in parallel with 2.2 nF from the gain node to the output.
notes: The circuit uses one channel, taken as channel A; channel B is unused.

circuits.title: Preamplifier for professional microphones powered from a 9-V battery
circuits.description: A portable balanced microphone preamplifier with high common-mode rejection, running from one 9 V battery at about 2 mA. The two OPA1692 channels make an instrumentation amplifier of two op amps whose gain runs from 6 dB to 40 dB on a 10 kΩ log potentiometer in series with 20 Ω. The four feedback resistors are a matched 1 kΩ array, because their match sets the common-mode rejection. An OPA171 buffers half the battery (two 100 kΩ resistors, 1 µF) as VBIAS, the mid-rail reference for the whole circuit. At the XLR input, two 6.8 kΩ resistors switch between 48 V phantom power and a 47 kΩ load to ground; 100 pF capacitors to the shell, 47 µF coupling capacitors, 2.2 kΩ + 2.2 kΩ with 22 kΩ to VBIAS for input bias, 68 Ω and 100 pF for RF filtering, D1 to D4 and a 10 V zener for ESD protection, and 30 Ω into each noninverting input. The output leaves through 68 Ω and 47 µF, with 47 kΩ to ground.

operation.text: OPA169x is a family of low-noise op amps in two- and four-channel versions, all stable at a gain of 1; the OPA1692 is the two-channel one. In each channel a folded-cascode input stage built for very low noise drives an output stage that swings rail to rail. A channel is made of a bipolar input pair with a tail current source, a pre-driver block with distortion cancellation, and the output transistors, with a compensation capacitor from the output back to the pre-driver input.

Lowering distortion with more loop gain normally costs supply current. The OPA169x instead cancels the odd-order harmonics that the input pair of transistors generates, at no extra current. Against three competing low-power amplifiers at similar supply current, its THD+N is more than 30 dB lower at high audio frequencies (Figure 53).
Overdriving the input beyond its common-mode limits does not flip the output to the opposite rail; the output simply clips at the rail it is heading for (Figures 51 and 54).

Each input and the output have steering diodes to the internal supply lines, which meet at an absorption (clamp) device between the rails; the inputs see 250 Ω in series inside the part. The clamp threshold sits between the normal operating voltage and the breakdown voltage, and once past it the clamp switches on quickly and holds the rail-to-rail voltage at a safe level during an ESD event. In normal use none of this conducts. If an input is driven 500 mV or more above V+, an upper steering diode conducts into V+; limit the current into that input to 10 mA. Should V+ be unable to sink the current, the input can end up powering the amplifier and lift the supply past its absolute maximum.

With the supplies at 0 V, a signal on an input feeds the amplifier through the steering diodes. High-impedance supplies leave the part in an abnormal bias state; low-impedance supplies can draw large current through the diodes, limited only by the source and any input resistance. Where the supply's ability to absorb this current is in doubt, zener diodes (or TVS parts) on the supply pins can be added; pick a zener voltage above the normal supply so it stays off, but low enough to conduct before the supply pin rises past its safe level.

The amplifiers work from ±1.75 V to ±18 V, that is 3.5 V to 36 V between the pins. The two supplies need not be equal: for instance +25 V and –5 V. The inputs must still be kept inside the specified common-mode range. Key parameters are guaranteed from –40 °C to 125 °C, and the typical curves show what changes strongly with supply or temperature.

Low closed-loop gain combined with a large capacitive load eats phase margin and can cause peaking or oscillation. A small series resistor at the output, for example RS = 50 Ω, isolates heavier capacitive loads.

Noise sources add as squares under a root: the amplifier voltage noise, its current noise times the source resistance, and the thermal noise of the source and feedback resistors. Voltage noise dominates at low source impedance; below 100 kΩ of source impedance the OPA169x current noise adds nothing worth counting (Figures 11 and 56). In gain circuits the feedback resistors add thermal noise and current-noise terms; low values keep these small, but too low a value loads the output.

EMIRR IN+ rates how far RF driven into the + input moves the offset voltage; a higher figure in dB means better immunity. The noninverting input is the one characterized: the inputs are the pins most prone to rectify RF, the two inputs are laid out symmetrically and behave about the same, and the noninverting pin can be driven alone on a board. RF on any pin beyond the loop bandwidth (5.1 MHz) can cause DC offsets or transients, so sensitive analog nodes need shielding and distance from radio signals and from digital clocks and buses. In the test the RF source drives the noninverting input through a 50 Ω line; the amplifier is a unity-gain buffer whose output is filtered by a low-pass network and read by a sampling multimeter; the supplies are bypassed with 0.1 µF and 10 µF; the RF is unmodulated, 0 V DC bias, swept over 201 log-spaced points at 25 °C. The input mismatch reflection is measured and accounted for.
A noisy or high-impedance supply needs bypass capacitors right at the pins; 0.1 µF is enough in most cases.

Place a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor from each supply pin to ground as close to the part as possible; on a single supply only V+ needs one. Keep analog and digital grounds apart and follow the ground current; a ground plane on an inner layer spreads heat and cuts EMI pickup. Route the inputs away from supply and output traces, crossing them at right angles where they must meet. Put the feedback and gain resistors (RF, RG) right next to the inverting-input pin to cut stray capacitance, and keep input runs short, since the inputs are the most sensitive nodes. Leakage from nearby traces at other voltages can be cut with a guard ring, driven from a low impedance, round the critical traces. Clean the board after assembly; after aqueous cleaning, bake it (85 °C for 30 minutes is enough in most cases) to drive moisture out of the plastic package.

The amplifiers can drive 2 kΩ on up to ±18 V across the full temperature range; dissipation rises with supply voltage. The copper lead frame conducts heat better than ordinary lead frames. Wide copper traces act as a heat sink, and a part soldered to the board runs cooler than one in a socket.
The built-in ESD protection is limited: store and handle the parts with the leads shorted together or in conductive foam.
